title: What's this? Things around you
goal: Point at things near and far, make plurals with *-lar*, put adjectives in front of nouns, and enjoy the fact that Uzbek has no *a*, no *the*, and no grammatical gender.
bekal: ask *Bu nima?* and answer it with one word
tell apart *bu* (this), *shu* (that, nearby), and *u* (that, far away)
attach *-lar* for the plural, and know when it is **not** used

dialogs.title: Dialog — Yotoqxonadagi xona
dialogs.intro: Nilufar shows Budi to his new dorm room. She points at things one by one, as if giving him his first lesson.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Bu stol, bu esa stul. Ular yangi.
lines.id: This is a table, and this is a chair. Both are new.
lines.literal: this table, this as-for chair. they new.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: U nima? U yerda, derazaning yonida.
lines.id: What's that? Over there, by the window.
lines.literal: that what? that place-at, window-of side-its-at.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: U kitob javoni. Bu yerda kitoblar bor.
lines.id: That's a bookshelf. There are books here.
lines.literal: that book shelf-its. this place-at books there-are.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Ha, hammasi oʻzbekcha. Bu lugʻat, bular darsliklar.
lines.id: Yes, they're all in Uzbek. This is a dictionary, and these are textbooks.
lines.literal: yes, all-of-them Uzbek-language. this dictionary, these lesson-books.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Is the dictionary old or new?

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Eski, lekin juda yaxshi. U qimmat emas.
lines.id: Old, but very good. It's not expensive.
lines.literal: old, but very good. it expensive not.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: I'm glad. Here's the key — it's yours.

notes: **No a, an, or the.** *Kitob* can mean "book", "a book", or "the book" — context decides. If you really need to stress "that book", just point: *bu kitob*, *shu kitob*, *u kitob*.
**Bu esa means "and this one, on the other hand".** The little word *esa* contrasts two things in a row: *Bu stol, bu esa stul*. It's polite, neutral, and very common in writing.
**Hammasi = "all of them".** The root *hamma* (all) plus the ending *-si* ("its/their"). You'll meet that ending again in unit 3, where it becomes one of the most important tools in Uzbek.
**Yoki means "or", and either-or questions use -mi twice.** *Eskimi yoki yangimi?* — literally "old-? or new-?". Uzbek puts the question marker on both choices, whereas English asks only once.
**Sizniki means "yours" as a standalone word.** *Bu sizniki* = "This is yours". The pattern: pronoun + *-niki*. So *meniki* (mine), *seniki*, *uniki*, *bizniki*, *sizniki*, *ularniki*.

grammars.title: Bu, shu, u — three distances, not two
body: English has "this" and "that". Uzbek adds one step in the middle, and once you see the pattern, it's easy.

head: Bentuk
Say it
Distance
Example
rows: this — in your hand, right in front of you

after: Look at the last row: **u and ular also mean "he/she" and "they"**. Uzbek doesn't separate people and things here. *U kim?* = "Who is he/she?"; *U nima?* = "What is that?". Only the question word tells them apart.
*Shu* is the safest choice when you mean something **just mentioned in the conversation**, rather than something you're pointing at. In English both are simply "that".
For places, all three take the word *yer* (place): *bu yerda* (here), *shu yerda* (right there), *u yerda* (over there). You'll see these constantly from unit 4 on.

grammars.title: -lar for plurals, and adjectives that never change
body: Two short rules that save you months compared with Russian or French.
after: **Adjectives always come before the noun, and they never change form.** *Katta uy*, *katta uylar*, *katta uyda* — *katta* stays *katta* forever. No agreement in gender, number, or case as in Russian or French.

⚠️ **After a number, -lar is dropped.** *Uch kitob* (three books), not *uch kitoblar*. It makes sense: the number already shows how many, so marking it twice is seen as redundant. Turkish works the same way.
*-lar* is also used to show respect: *ustozlar keldilar* = "The teacher has come" (one person, but made plural as a sign of respect). You'll see this habit again in unit 10.

blocks.text: Point at each object in your room right now and say its name out loud. Ten minutes now saves ten hours later.

Four of these come from Russian and have barely changed: *stol*, *stul*, *ruchka*, *sumka*. Uzbekistan spent seventy years in the Soviet Union, and it shows most in words for modern things — *avtobus*, *magazin*, *kompyuter*, *bank*, *pochta*. If you don't know a modern noun, try the Russian one; chances are good it's the right word.
Eight pairs of opposites. Learning them in pairs is much faster than one at a time.
⚠️ Note **qimmat**: it means **expensive**. Its root is the Arabic word for "value" (*qīma*), so literally "of high value".
To strengthen an adjective, just put *juda* (very) in front: *juda katta*, *juda arzon*, *juda chiroyli*. To soften it, use *biroz* (a bit): *biroz qimmat* = a bit expensive.
